newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn ready for compromise on social chapter - Kinkel.
newsitem.headline: Bonn ready for compromise on social chapter - Kinkel.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Wednesday Bonn was not opposed to adding a jobs chapter to the Maastricht treaty and, signalling a possible policy change, he said Germany was ready for compromise.

Kinkel's remarks came after deputies from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition called on Bonn to withdraw its long-standing opposition to an employment chapter to the treaty at an EU summit in Amsterdam next week.
He told the Maerkische Oderzeitung newspaper in an interview that European Union states should do their utmost to fight joblessness and he was sure negotiations were making progress.
"Of course we are not opposed to a jobs chapter. It is obvious that everything possible must be done to counteract the intolerably high level of unemployment," Kinkel said.
"The only question is: how can this be done successfully? Negotiations (on a jobs chapter) in Brussels are making progress. We are open to a compromise," he said.
Germany had opposed the idea of a jobs chapter for years fearing political interference in the work of a future independent European central bank.

But Kinkel's comments suggested the government might be favourable to Tuesday's proposals by parliamentary deputies in Kohl's coalition and that Germany might be ready to bend to French pressure on the issue.

At a meeting of European economic and finance ministers in Luxembourg this week, the new leftist French government put the brakes on European economic and monetary union (EMU), saying it needed time to think before signing a stability pact aimed at guaranteeing the stability of the single currency.
The draft paper of the German coalition parties also said tighter coordination of jobs policies on the part of EU members could be possible without transferring additional powers to Brussels.
This could also include a sharper orientation of the European social fund towards jobs-related projects.
